awa001.description: Shailendra Kumar Mishra, a farmer from Allahabad, Uttar Pradesh, India, talks about farming in his village in the Allahabadi variety of Awadhi. He says which crops his family grows through the year and how they make paneer from milk. Subhashish Panigrahi interviewed him on 25 July 2026 for OpenSpeaks Archives, with support from Abhinav Srivastava of Azad Reads and Harsha Vardhan Mishra.
awa001.title: Illahabadi-Awadhi documentation: Discussion on agriculture
bfw001.description: Gobardhan Panda, a researcher of the Bonda language, recites the Bonda origin myth as a poem he wrote in Bonda, and translates the stanzas into Odia. Prateek Pattanaik recorded it in 2018 for Remosam, a 2019 documentary by Subhashish Panigrahi. The footage wasn't used in the film, and it was edited and published under the Munaremo project in 2024. Subtitles are by Gobardhan Panda and Subhashish Panigrahi.
bfw001.title: Story
bfw002.description: Gobardhan Panda, a self-taught anthropologist from Koraput, Odisha, India, points to parts of the body and names them in Bonda. Prateek Pattanaik recorded it in 2018 for Remosam, a 2019 documentary by Subhashish Panigrahi. The footage wasn't used in the film, and it was edited and published under the Munaremo project in 2024. Subtitles are by Subhashish Panigrahi, using Panda's 1998 book Remosam as a reference.
bfw002.title: Body parts
bfw003.description: Mangala Sisa, a Bonda speaker, and Gobardhan Panda, an anthropologist and researcher, talk about making pendom, a drink like handia, and drink it together. They also talk about how it was drunk at Pus Porob, a festival that had just ended. They speak Bonda with some Desia, which is marked in 'single quotes' in the subtitles. Prateek Pattanaik recorded it in 2018 for Remosam, a 2019 documentary by Subhashish Panigrahi. A short part was used in the film, and the longer version was edited and published under the Munaremo project in 2024. Subtitles are by Gobardhan Panda and Subhashish Panigrahi, using Panda's 1998 book Remosam as a reference.
bfw003.title: Pendom
bfw004.description: Sukra Dhangdamajhi, a disari (Bonda shaman) from Malkangiri district, Odisha, India, talks about his practice. Gobardhan Panda, a researcher of the Bonda language, interviews him in Bonda with some Desia, the common language of the Bonda, Gutob, Odia and other local communities. Desia words are marked in quotes in the Odia subtitles, such as 'ନି-ନା, ସେରମୂଲ୍'. Prateek Pattanaik recorded it in 2018 for Remosam, a 2019 documentary by Subhashish Panigrahi. Part of the footage was used in the film, and Panigrahi edited and published it under the Munaremo project in 2024. Gobardhan Panda subtitled the Bonda in Odia, and Panigrahi translated the subtitles into English and edited the Odia.
bfw004.title: Shamanism
gbm001.description: Sampati, a Jaunpuri speaker from Dewalsari in the Garhwal region of Uttarakhand, India, talks about Aadhaar and access to public information. Jaunpuri is a dialect of Garhwali. Subhashish Panigrahi interviewed Sampati on 8 November 2019 for his 2021 documentary MarginalizedAadhaar. Panigrahi edited unused or trimmed footage from the film and published it under the OpenSpeaks Archives project in 2026. Hindi subtitles are by Arun Gour and Manoj Bilwal, edited by Panigrahi.
gbm001.title: Information access and Aadhaar
gbm002.description: Surendra Dutt, a Jaunpuri speaker from Bangseel, Uttarakhand, India, talks about the state of his farming. Subhashish Panigrahi interviewed and recorded him there in 2019 for his 2021 documentary MarginalizedAadhaar. Hindi subtitles are by Arun Gour, edited by Panigrahi.
gbm002.title: Current state of farming

hoc002.description: Mangal Singhku, a Ho speaker, describes Guan Bunga, a ceremony of the Ho community of India. Subhashish Panigrahi recorded it at Keshpada, Mayurbhanj district, Odisha, India, for his 2019 documentary Mage Porob. Panigrahi edited several videos that were unused or little used in the film into one short documentary, published under the 𑢼𑣃𑣃𑣊 𑢾𑣁𑣌𑣁𑣖 (Ruum Sakam) project in 2024. Ho subtitles are by Ganesh Birua, the Odia translation is by Panigrahi, and the English translation is by Birua and Panigrahi, edited by Panigrahi.

kfy001.description: Surendra Singh Pangtey introduces himself in Johari, a dialect of Kumaoni. Pangtey is an author and a former Indian Army and Indian Administrative Service officer. He speaks two main forms of Johari. One was used mostly in the past in very particular settings, such as when two Shauka riders greet each other as their horses pass. It uses many words from Rankas and Shaukiya-Khun, older forms that are no longer spoken. The other, known as Johari, is what the Shauka people use in everyday conversation. This video is from Johari (जोहारी), a 2026 short film by Subhashish Panigrahi in OpenSpeaks Archives, made from footage recorded for his 2021 documentary MarginalizedAadhaar. Subtitles are by Pangtey, edited by Panigrahi.

kip001.description: Tika Kumari Budha, a childhood development trainer from Jungkot, Rolpa district, Nepal, speaks in Sheshi Kham, a variety of Kham Magar. She talks about her family's farming year: corn sown in Jeth (Jyeshtha) and Baisakh, barley and wheat in November and December, and mustard and millet. Women wove aloe fibre into thread and mats while men sowed and ploughed, and in winter many men went to Butwal, Bhairawa, Kathmandu, India or other countries to earn money. Uday Raj Aaley interviewed her and Deewash Thapa recorded the interview in Jungkot on 17 July 2026 for OpenSpeaks Archives. Sheshi Kham and Nepali subtitles are by Budha, transcribed and typed by Aaley, and the English translation is by Subhashish Panigrahi, who also edited the video.
kip001.title: Sheshi Kham language documentation

mjw-w1.description: Words in Karbi spoken by Dharamsing Teron, cut from his interview with Subhashish Panigrahi on 21 May 2017.
mjw-w1.title: Karbi words
mjw001.description: Dharamsing Teron (D.S. Teron), a Karbi speaker from Karbi Anglong district, Assam, India, says how his name is pronounced in Karbi and explains how Karbi family names are given. Subhashish Panigrahi interviewed him remotely, with his permission, on 21 May 2017. This is part 1 of the nine-part interview, and mjw010 is the full recording.
mjw001.title: Pronunciation of interviewee's name
mjw002.description: Dharamsing Teron explains the meaning of the word "Karbi" and talks about the Karbi people, and about the local legends that guide their daily life, beliefs and social activities. Subhashish Panigrahi interviewed him remotely, with his permission, on 21 May 2017. This is part 2 of the nine-part interview, and mjw010 is the full recording.
mjw002.title: Meaning of Karbi and the Karbi people
mjw003.description: Dharamsing Teron talks about Jor Teron, the village where he was born. It's named after his grandfather, a local community leader who founded the village. Subhashish Panigrahi interviewed him remotely, with his permission, on 21 May 2017. This is part 3 of the nine-part interview, and mjw010 is the full recording.
mjw003.title: Interviewee D.S. Teron's birthplace Jor Teron
mjw004.description: Dharamsing Teron talks about his childhood in the 1960s and how the Karbi people lived then. He describes two games: walking on stilts so that thorns don't pierce bare feet on swampy ground, and Hambi (IPA /haːmbi/), played with locally grown nickernuts. In Hambi, two teams with the same number of players, at least two each, stand about five metres apart. The game has stages, each with its own name, and the players tease the other team. Subhashish Panigrahi interviewed him remotely, with his permission, on 21 May 2017. This is part 4 of the nine-part interview, and mjw010 is the full recording.
mjw004.title: Traditional games of the Karbi people
mjw005.description: Dharamsing Teron talks about how Karbi has influenced other languages and been influenced by them. He cites linguists who relate Karbi to the Kukish or Kuki-Chin languages (IPA /kuki t͡ʃin/) and to Naga, Meitei, Garo and Khasi. Assamese is the most recent influence, as the Karbi people came into closer contact with Assamese speakers during and after 1947. Subhashish Panigrahi interviewed him remotely, with his permission, on 21 May 2017. This is part 5 of the nine-part interview, and mjw010 is the full recording.
mjw005.title: Karbi language - its language family and related languages
mjw006.description: Dharamsing Teron tells a Karbi story from the Jor Teron region, with an introduction and conclusion in English. The introduction starts at 01:55, the story in Karbi runs from 04:33 to 11:19, and the conclusion follows. The story, "Votia temo" (IPA /ot̪iaː t̪emɔ/), is about a hen (vo means bird in Karbi) who lives with a cat, a pig, a dog and a duck. The hen always finds and cooks the food while the others never help, and the story tells how she deals with them. Subhashish Panigrahi interviewed him remotely, with his permission, on 21 May 2017. This is part 6 of the nine-part interview, and mjw010 is the full recording.
mjw006.title: Storytelling of the Karbi people
mjw007.description: Dharamsing Teron talks with Subhashish Panigrahi about Karbi folk songs and sings part of an old love ballad. He introduces the song in English from 02:15, sings from 02:35 to 03:13, and talks about it afterwards. Panigrahi interviewed him remotely, with his permission, on 21 May 2017. This is part 7 of the nine-part interview, and mjw010 is the full recording.
mjw007.title: Folk songs of the Karbi people
mjw008.description: Dharamsing Teron describes Cho Mang Kan (IPA /t͡ʃo maːŋg kaːn/), a funeral festival held a few years after a death. It lasts three to five days and is expensive, so families take their time to decide when to hold it. The whole community takes part, especially young men and women, and the songs are openly erotic, which the community accepts. From 04:45 to 06:48 he describes in Karbi the procession, in which people of all ages carry the Jambili Athon (IPA /d͡ʒaːmbili aːt̪ʰɔn/), the Karbi emblem. It's a wooden pole of Bengwoi ke-er (Wrightia coccinea) topped with a carved bird, the Voraju (IPA /boraːd͡ʒu/, greater racket-tailed drongo), and each village has its own. Drummers play while young people sing and dance, and the gatherings drew 400 to 1,000 people, who feasted, drank local liquor and teased each other. He introduces the festival in English up to 04:45 and sums up in English after 06:48. On the Jambili Athon, see Robindra Teron, "Traditional woodcraft, Jambili Athon of the Karbis", Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge 7(1), January 2008, pp. 103–107. Subhashish Panigrahi interviewed him remotely, with his permission, on 21 May 2017. This is part 8 of the nine-part interview, and mjw010 is the full recording.
mjw008.title: Local festival celebrations by the Karbi people
mjw009.description: Dharamsing Teron describes his daily activities in Karbi from 00:41 to 03:48 and then explains them in English. Subhashish Panigrahi interviewed him remotely, with his permission, on 21 May 2017. This is part 9 of the nine-part interview, and mjw010 is the full recording.
mjw009.title: Daily activities of the interviewee
mjw010.description: The full 53-minute interview with Dharamsing Teron (D.S. Teron), a Karbi speaker from Karbi Anglong district, Assam, India. It covers the introduction and his name (00:00–01:48), the meaning of "Karbi" (01:48–03:27), his birthplace (03:27–04:18) and children's games (04:18–08:52). It then moves to the Karbi language (08:52–15:09), storytelling (15:09–27:21), a folk song (27:21–31:03), festivals (31:03–42:30) and his daily activities (42:30–52:37). Subhashish Panigrahi interviewed him remotely, with his permission, on 21 May 2017. mjw001 to mjw009 are the same interview in nine parts.
mjw010.title: Full interview with Karbi language speaker D.S. Teron

Subhashish Panigrahi recorded her in Balasore (Baleshwar), Odisha, India, on 12 January 2014, while making his 2022 documentary Nani Ma, and published this shorter edit on Wikimedia Commons the same day. ory002.title: Bahuna gita
ory003.description: The late Musamoni Panigrahi tells a bedtime story in the Baleswari dialect of Odia. Set in the British Raj, it is about a newly widowed woman who isn't allowed to say her husband's name, and who twists her words to tell the judge about her family before she cremates him. Subhashish Panigrahi recorded her in Balasore (Baleshwar), Odisha, India, on 20 January 2014, while making his 2022 documentary Nani Ma, and published it on Wikimedia Commons the same day. Odia and English subtitles are on Commons.

pcj001.description: Balaram Muduli, a Gorum speaker from Odisha, India, introduces himself and talks about the lack of teachers who can teach in Gorum. Opino Gomango, a Sora speaker, interviewed him in Bhubaneswar, Odisha, on 1 March 2026. Gomango subtitled the interview in English on location from Muduli's word-for-word Odia translation. Subhashish Panigrahi edited the footage and subtitles and published them under the OpenSpeaks Archives project in 2026.

rji001.description: Kaliprasad Raji, a Raji speaker from Bardiya district, Nepal, introduces himself and talks about how Raji is used every day. Uday Raj Aaley interviewed him at his home in Nepal on 25 February 2026. Aaley subtitled the interview in Nepali on location from Raji's word-for-word Nepali translation. Subhashish Panigrahi edited the footage and subtitles and published them under the OpenSpeaks Archives project in 2026.
rji001.title: Introduction and use of Raji
rji002.description: Kaliprasad Raji, a Raji speaker from Bardiya district, Nepal, talks about how Raji is used every day, especially among young people. Uday Raj Aaley interviewed him in his village in Nepal on 25 February 2026. Aaley subtitled the interview in Nepali on location from Raji's word-for-word Nepali translation. Subhashish Panigrahi edited the footage and subtitles and published them under the OpenSpeaks Archives project in 2026.
rji002.title: Current use of Raji by speakers
rji003.description: Kaliprasad Raji, a fluent Raji speaker, says "Raji bhasha" ("राजी भाषा", Raji language). The clip is cut from Uday Raj Aaley's video interview with him for OpenSpeaks Archives, recorded at his home in Bardiya district, Nepal, on 25 February 2026. In it, Raji introduces himself and talks about how Raji is used every day. Aaley subtitled the interview in Nepali on location from Raji's word-for-word Nepali translation.

rnp001.description: Bimla Badwal and K.S. Badwal, a married couple who speak the Marcha dialect of Rongpo, talk in Marcha about the past in each other's home towns. Subhashish Panigrahi interviewed them in 2019 for his 2021 documentary MarginalizedAadhaar. Panigrahi edited unused or trimmed footage from the film and published it under the OpenSpeaks Archives project in 2025. Hindi subtitles are by Kimmi Pal, a Rongpo speaker and OpenSpeaks Fellow, with advice from Bhawani Pal and edits by Panigrahi, and the English translation is by Panigrahi.
rnp001.title: Nostalgic past

Panigrahi edited unused or trimmed footage from the film and published it under the OpenSpeaks Archives project in 2025. Hindi subtitles are by Kimmi Pal, a Rongpo speaker and OpenSpeaks Fellow, with advice from Bhawani Pal and edits by Panigrahi, and the English translation is by Panigrahi.

sci001.description: Sajehan Buckman, a Sri Lanka Malay speaker from Colombo, Sri Lanka, talks about where his community came from and its migration from present-day Indonesia and Malaysia to Sri Lanka. Subhashish Panigrahi and Omar Rajaraman interviewed him in Colombo on 19 February 2026. English subtitles are by Panigrahi, edited by Ramzy Muliawan.

srb001.description: Ramani Dalbehera, a Lanjia Sora speaker from Rayagada district, Odisha, India, talks about her experience of Aadhaar, India's biometric ID. Opino Gomango and Subhashish Panigrahi interviewed her in 2019 for Panigrahi's 2021 documentary MarginalizedAadhaar. Gomango asked the questions in Sora, building on Panigrahi's broader questions in Odia, with Namad Dalbehera, a Lanjia Sora speaker related to Ramani, present. Panigrahi edited unused or trimmed footage from the film and published it under the OpenSpeaks Archives project in 2026. English subtitles are by Gomango, and the edits and Odia subtitles are by Panigrahi.
srb001.title: Aadhaar Experience
srb002.description: Ramani Dalbehera, a Lanjia Sora speaker from Rayagada district, Odisha, India, talks about the difficulty of getting her Aadhaar data corrected. Opino Gomango interviewed her in 2019.
